newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany will work with Britain, France on satellite.
newsitem.headline: Germany will work with Britain, France on satellite.

text.p: The German army will work together with France and Britain to build up a network of communications satellites by the middle of the next decade, a spokesman for the German Defence Ministry said on Saturday.

Confirming a report to appear in Monday's edition of Der Spiegel news magazine, the Defence Ministry spokesman said the communications satellites were needed to improve army leaders' abilities to communicate with units in the field.
The upgraded communications capabilities are in particular needed for the German army's missions abroad, he said. Currently, the army rents satellites for its international communications.
The satellite system to be jointly developed with France and Britain should be functional by the year 2005, the spokesman said.

Der Spiegel said the Defence ministry had already budgeted about 200 million marks for the development of the satellites, that it said would cost more than a billion marks. The magazine said Daimler-Benz Aerospace (DASA) was among the companies that would be working on the development.
But the Defence Ministry spokesman declined to comment on the figures.
France and Germany are also exploring working on another joint project to build a new spy satellite, called Helios 2.
French Defence Minister Charles Millon said last week Paris was not prepared to postpone the spy satellite project which Bonn is having trouble financing.
The planned development of Helios 2 is expected to cost six or seven billion marks over the next 13 years.
German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe says he cannot afford Bonn's share of the satellite from his own 1997 budget, cut four percent from its planned level as part of an austerity programme.

France wants to make Europe less dependent on United States intelligence by building the Helios 2 satellite, and sees the project, which Chancellor Kohl agreed to in talks with President Jacques Chirac, as a flagship of Franco-German cooperation.
